sections.label: The money terms
sections.h2: Three numbers that decide whether the business lives.
body: Everything spent to win one customer, divided by the customers won. Ads, wages, tools, time. If it costs $180 to win a customer, that is your CAC. New reps think the sale is free because they did not write the check.
What a customer is worth over the whole relationship, not the first order. A $60 a month customer who stays two years is worth $1,440. LTV against CAC tells you whether growing is smart or suicidal.
The one thing you ask the person to do next. Not three things. One. In a post, in a text, at the end of a conversation. If you cannot say what the CTA was, there was not one.

Most reps can tell you the price. Fewer can tell you what it cost to get the customer in front of them, or what that customer is worth over two years. Those two numbers decide everything the price does not.

sections.label: The conversation terms
body: The questions that find the customer's actual problem before you present anything. The sale is made here. Skip it and you get 'let me think about it.'

A small question that gets agreement on one point before moving on. 'That makes sense, right?' Used well, it keeps the customer with you. Used every sentence, it sounds like a script and people feel it.
The moment the customer shows they are ready: a deeper question, future talk, 'how soon.' Two of them and you stop presenting and ask. Most reps miss the signal and keep talking.
'Thursday or Saturday?' Both answers are a yes. It removes the yes-or-no decision for the customer who is on the fence. It does not work on someone who has not been through discovery.
A tie-down every sentence is a script. A tie-down at the right moment is a conversation. New reps learn the words before they learn the timing, and the timing is the whole skill.

sections.label: The floor terms
sections.h2: Three terms for face to face and phone.
body: Face to face, how far away a customer decides whether to engage with you: usually before you have said a word. Body language, energy and position do the work at ten feet. The words only matter once they are at three.
Telling the customer what is about to happen before it happens. 'I am going to ask two questions, then show you one thing.' It lowers resistance because nobody is being ambushed.

What you say after the yes so it stays a yes. Reframe the choice, confirm the next step, tell them exactly what happens next. Buyer's remorse starts in the silence after the sale, and the lock fills it.
The sale is not over when they say yes. It is over when they know exactly what happens next and why they made a good call. The silence after the yes is where deals die.

Give this to a rep to run on themselves, or run it with them.
prompt: Quiz me on ten sales terms, one at a time: CAC, LTV, CTA, discovery, tie-down, ready signal, the two-option ask, approach distance, pre-frame, and the lock. 1. Ask me to explain each one in my own words and give one example from my own work. 2. After each answer, score it 1 to 3: 1 means I could not explain it, 2 means I explained it but the example was weak, 3 means I could teach it. 3. Do not correct me mid-quiz. At the end, give me the three terms to study, the one I explained best, and one coaching note in two sentences. My medium is [face to face / phone / meetings].
